podcast.title: Band Breakup
podcast.body: After the success and subsequent liability of "Toast," Street Band released a half dozen more "straight ahead rock and roll singles" which were "miserable failures." The band eventually broke up for good in 1979 and "descended into obscurity," save for the single song "Toast" and keyboardist Paul Young's subsequent solo career. "And Street Band broke up for good in 1979 and descended into obscurity."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Formation
podcast.body: Street Band was a five-piece group formed in England in 1977. "This was a five piece formed in England back in 1977."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Impact of "Toast" on Band Credibility
podcast.body: The unexpected success of "Toast" significantly damaged Street Band's credibility. Audiences who came to see them, expecting a quirky English outfit based on the song, were instead met with a loud, conventional rock band, leading to a disconnect that hurt their career. "When people came out to see Street Band, they expected some quirky English outfit and said they got this loud, fairly conventional rock band. So essentially, toast destroyed their credibility completely."

xref.title: Toast (1978) – Novelty B-Side That Became a Hit During the UK Baker's Strike, Launched by Street Band
xref.body: Released as the B-side to "Hold On" by Street Band, a straight-ahead UK rock group, "Toast" was a song about the joys of making toast, recorded when the band needed filler. During the Baker's Strike of the late 1970s, someone at the BBC discovered the track and put it on air; it became an unexpected quirky hit, but branded the band as novelty artists, leading to their breakup. One member of Street Band was Paul Young, who went on to have major multi-platinum success as a blue-eyed soul singer in the 1980s. "Street Band, with a song called Toast from 1978. Naturally, they were soon branded as a novelty act and they broke up shortly thereafter."

xref.title: Performance with Springsteen at Pinkpop Festival (2009)
xref.body: The Killers performed with Bruce Springsteen at the 2009 Pinkpop Festival in the Netherlands, with Brandon Flowers joining Springsteen and the E Street Band on stage to sing "Thunder Road" after The Killers' own set. "The killers played right before Springsteen, and Brandon was brought back on during the East Street band set to sing Thunder Road."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bruce Springsteen & The E Street Band Fill-in
xref.body: After graduating high school in 2008, Jay filled in as drummer for Bruce Springsteen's E Street Band when his father, Max Weinberg, had a scheduling conflict with the Conan O'Brien show. "So, who did Springsteen call the fill-in? Son Jay."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Highest-Grossing Reunion Tour of All Time (Projected)
xref.body: The Oasis reunion tour is projected to become the highest-grossing reunion tour in history, surpassing previous records set by bands such as The Police, Led Zeppelin, The E Street Band, Genesis, and Black Sabbath. "I don't know, whatever you want to compare it to, this will be the highest grossing reunion tour of all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Large Band Composition
xref.body: Arcade Fire is noted for having a large number of members who play a wide array of different instruments, drawing a comparison to the expansive lineup of Bruce Springsteen's E Street Band. "Like Springsteen's East Street band, Arcade Fire has a lot of members playing a lot of different instruments."

xref.title: Solo Career Post-Street Band
xref.body: Following the breakup of Street Band in 1979, keyboardist Paul Young embarked on a successful solo career. He achieved significant success with a series of hit singles throughout the early and middle 1980s. "Save for this one song. And for one member, keyboardist Paul Young went on to a solo career and did very well with the series of hit singles to the early and middle 1980s."
